Forrest Bowers, Director

Doug Vincent-Lang, Commissioner

Soldotna Office 43961 K Beach Rd. Soldotna Ak. 99669

Juneau, AK 99811-5526

Advisory Announcement For Immediate Release: November 24, 2026

CONTACT: Lee Borden, Area Management Biologist Colton Lipka, Regional Management Coordinator Office: (907) 262-9368

2026 Upper Cook Inlet Commercial Salmon Fishery Season Summary

The following is an overview of the 2026 Upper Cook Inlet (UCI) commercial salmon season. All data are preliminary. The preliminary 2026 UCI sockeye salmon total run of 4.7 million fish was 38% below the preseason forecast of 7.6 million fish (Table 1). The commercial harvest of 1.2 million salmon was 58% less than the recent 20-year average annual harvest of 3.0 million fish (Table 2). The 2026 exvessel value of all salmon species was $16.2 million, 32% less than the previous 20-year average annual exvessel value of $23.8 million (Table 3). Of the five Pacific salmon species harvested in UCI, sockeye salmon accounted for 94% of the total exvessel value in 2026, near the recent 20-year average of 92% (Table 3). The 2026 king salmon harvest of 137 fish is the 2nd lowest on record. Low commercial king salmon harvest reflects low abundance trends and a conservative management approach. Overall participation in UCI was lower than in previous years, with 678 permits making deliveries, 21% below the 20-year average of 856 permits (Tables 4 and 5).

All UCI-monitored sockeye salmon escapement and inriver goals were met or exceeded in 2026 except for the Judd Lake sustainable escapement goal (SEG). Larson Lake was within the SEG range. The Kasilof River exceeded the biological escapement goal range (BEG). The Kenai River sockeye salmon late-run was within the inriver goal range (IRG). The Chelatna Lake weir was not operated in 2026 due to high water conditions throughout the season (Table 6).

In 2026, the Kenai River early-run large king salmon optimal escapement goal (OEG) was not achieved. The Kenai River late-run large king salmon recovery goal (RG), OEG, and SEG were not achieved. Of the three southern Kenai Peninsula king salmon systems with escapement goals, the SEG was achieved at the Anchor River and not achieved for Ninilchik River natural-origin king salmon. The Deep Creek king salmon run was not assessed due to lack of funding. In the Northern Cook Inlet region, the Little Susitna River king salmon SEG was not achieved, and the Deshka River king salmon BEG was not achieved. King salmon escapements for the Susitna River Drainage are currently undergoing post-season analysis, but preliminary aerial survey results indicate low king salmon abundance (Table 6).

In 2026, coho salmon were not assessed at the Deshka River due to the weir being rendered inoperable during July floods. The coho salmon SEG for Jim Creek and Fish Creek were both exceeded. The Little Susitna River coho salmon SEG was not achieved. The chum salmon SEG for Clear Creek in Chinitna Bay was not achieved (Table 6).

1

SOCKEYE SALMON

2026 Run and Fishery Summary In 2026, approximately 7.6 million sockeye salmon were forecasted to return to the UCI. Of these, 4.6 million sockeye salmon were estimated to be available for harvest, including commercial, sport, and personal use fisheries. The preliminary total run estimate for UCI sockeye salmon in 2026, which includes both harvest and escapement estimates, is 4.7 million fish (Table 1). This total run estimate is 2.9 million fish, or 38%, below forecast. Individual stock performance ranged from Fish Creek returning 84% above forecast to the Kenai River returning 52% below forecast (Table 1).

The end of season passage estimated at the river mile 19 sonar of 1,111,686 sockeye salmon exceeded the Kenai River sockeye salmon middle-tier inriver goal range (1,100,000–1,400,000 fish) (Table 6). In 2026, the midpoint of sockeye salmon passage occurred on July 25, which is 3 days earlier than the previous 20-year average midpoint (2006–2025).

The Kasilof River sockeye salmon sonar count of 1,055,564 fish exceeded the Kasilof River BEG of 140,000–320,000 fish (Table 6). The passage midpoint for Kasilof River sockeye salmon occurred on July 20, which was three days later than the 20-year average midpoint of July 17.

The 2026 total UCI commercial harvest of 947,259 sockeye salmon was 59% below the 2006– 2025 average annual harvest of 2.3 million fish (Table 2 and 5). Prices varied during the season but based on an estimated average price of $2.83 per pound, the total exvessel value of harvested sockeye salmon was $15.4 million. This is 29% less than the recent 20-year average value of $21.7 million and accounts for 94% of the total 2026 exvessel value of all salmon in UCI (Table 3).

East Side Set Net and Dip Net Fishery The Upper Subdistrict set gillnet fishery (ESSN) started and remained closed for the 2026 season due to a poor forecast of Kenai River late-run large king salmon (Figures 1 and 2).

The 2026 dip net commercial fishery preliminary harvest was 1 king, 62,444 sockeye, 4 coho, 398 pink, and 1 chum salmon. A total of 126 permits delivered fish from the commercial dip net fishery. (Table 4). Harvest was concentrated during the peak of the Kenai River sockeye salmon run from July 15 to July 31, and the highest success was on beaches near the mouth of the Kenai River.

Drift Gillnet Fishery The drift gillnet fishery management started the season under the provisions of the middle run size tier for Kenai River late-run sockeye salmon (2.3–4.6 million fish) based on the preseason forecast.

On July 27, the inseason projection of 3.0 million fish kept the management strategy at the middletier (> 4.6 million fish) regulations, maintaining the inriver run goal of 1.1–1.4 million fish. Unlike the ESSN fishery, the drift gillnet fishery is not as severely restricted for Kenai River late-run king salmon; instead, it is managed primarily to harvest UCI sockeye salmon and conservatively toward Northern Cook Inlet coho salmon. Beginning in 2024, the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) of Cook Inlet was managed directly by the National Marine Fisheries Service under a separate Federal Fisheries Management Plan. The remaining State of Alaska waters (SOA) were managed following stipulations in the Central District Drift Gillnet Fishery Management Plan (CDDGFMP 5 AAC 21.353; Figure 3). Commercial fishing was opened following the complex guidance of these plans via commercial periods in SOA waters primarily using prescribed drift gillnet areas, expanded corridor sections, and sockeye abundance triggers to guide commercial openings through the season.

2

From June 22 through September 11, the drift gillnet fleet fished a total of 35 days as follows: 5 days in the Expanded Kasilof and Anchor Point Section, 3 days in the Expanded Kenai/Kasilof Sections only, 6 days in the Ex. Kenai/Kasilof and Anchor Point Sections only, 4 days in Drift Gillnet Area 1 with some or all of the expanded sections, 1 day in Drift Gillnet Area 3, 10 days in Drift Gillnet Area 3 and 4, and 5 days district-wide in SOA waters. Beginning August 28, the Chinitna Bay Subdistrict was open to commercial drift and set gillnet fishing on Tuesdays and Fridays; harvest was recorded on 4 days. All UCI commercial drift gillnet fisheries were closed by EO on September 30 for the 2026 season.

The SOA waters drift gillnet fishery in UCI harvested 48 king, 207,396 sockeye, 28,896 coho, 19,277 pink, and 26,823 chum salmon for a total harvest of 282,440 salmon caught by 418 permits that made deliveries (Table 4).

The Federal waters drift gillnet fishery in UCI harvested 60 kings, 584,529 sockeye, 38,019 coho, 16,084 pink, and 53,784 chum salmon for a total harvest of 692,476 salmon caught by 359 permits that made deliveries (Table 4).

The total UCI drift gillnet harvest of 791,925 sockeye salmon was below the 20-year average harvest of 1,416,062 fish (Table 5). In 2026, 435 drift gillnet permits made deliveries for a season average harvest of approximately 1,821 sockeye salmon per permit. Participation was below the 20-year average of 421 drift gillnet permits (Tables 4 and 5).

Western and Chinitna Bay Subdistricts Fisheries The Western Subdistrict (Figures 1 and 2) set gillnet fishery opened for regulatory fishing periods on Thursday, June 18. The Chinitna Bay Subdistrict harvest is confidential due to the number of participants and processors. Approximately 16,288 sockeye salmon were harvested with set gillnet gear in the Western and Chinitna Bay Subdistricts. This was 59% below the average annual harvest of 39,564 fish during the most recent 20 years. Participation was below the 20-year average with 16 set gillnet permits making deliveries (Tables 4 and 5).

Kustatan Subdistrict Fishery The Kustatan Subdistrict includes those waters from the Drift River oil terminal to the Northern District boundary near the West Foreland (Figures 1 and 2). The 2026 fishery was closed from June 2 through June 12 by EO for conservation of Northern District king salmon. Approximately 6,132 sockeye salmon were harvested in the Kustatan Subdistrict in 2026, of which 749 sockeye salmon were harvested during the Big River fishery from June 12 through June 24. The 2026 sockeye salmon harvest for the Kustatan Subdistrict was 5% greater than the recent 20-year average harvest of 5,861 fish. Participation was greater than the 20-year average with 12 set gillnet permits making deliveries (Tables 4 and 5).

Kalgin Island Subdistrict Fishery The Kalgin Island Subdistrict (Figures 1 and 2) opened for regulatory Monday and Thursday fishing periods beginning June 25. In 2026, a total of 37,338 sockeye salmon were harvested from the Kalgin Island Subdistrict, with 4,399 of those fish taken during the Big River sockeye salmon fishery. The 2026 Kalgin Island Subdistrict harvest was 28% below the recent 20-year average harvest of 51,672 fish. Participation was at the 20-year average with 26 set gillnet permits making deliveries (Tables 4 and 5).

The Packers Creek video weir was not operated, and the SEG (15,000–30,000) was not assessed in 2026 (Table 6). The project is not expected to be operated in the future.

3

Northern District Fishery The Northern District (Figure 4) opened for sockeye salmon on June 29, after the directed king salmon fishery (May 25–June 24) and the regular period on June 25 was closed for king salmon conservation. In response to weak coho salmon abundance at the Little Susitna weir, commercial salmon fishing with set gillnets in the Northern District was closed effective 7:00 a.m. Monday, August 6, 2026. In 2026, a total of 33,132 sockeye salmon were harvested in the Northern District. This harvest was 23% below the recent 20-year average harvest of 42,885 sockeye salmon. Participation was below the 20-year average, with 63 set gillnet permits making deliveries (Tables 4 and 5).

COHO SALMON

2026 Run and Fishery Summary The 2026 commercial harvest estimate of 92,765 coho salmon in UCI was 41% below the recent 20-year average of 158,190 fish (Tables 2, 4, and 5). The 2026 drift gillnet harvest of 66,915 coho salmon was 26% below the recent 20-year average of 90,263 fish. The Northern District set gillnet fishery harvested 10,010 coho salmon, which was 72% below the recent 20-year average of 35,450 fish (Tables 4 and 5). State-managed coho salmon fisheries required conservative management in 2026, in part, because the federal total allowable catch and acceptable biological catch for coho salmon were both significantly exceeded during the 2026 federal salmon fishery in the United States Exclusive Economic Zone of Cook Inlet.

Based on an average price per pound of $0.83, the estimated exvessel value of the 2026 commercial coho salmon fishery was $447,405, or 2.7% of the total exvessel value of all species in Upper Cook Inlet. This was 37% below the recent 20-year average exvessel value of $709,950 for coho salmon in UCI (Table 3).

In UCI, there are four coho salmon systems with escapement goals. The Little Susitna River, Deshka River, and Fish Creek are monitored by weirs, while McRoberts Creek was assessed with foot surveys.

The Little Susitna weir began operating on May 17, the last day of counts was on September 23. The weir count of 1,768 fish did not achieve the SEG of 9,200–17,700 fish (Table 6).

The Deshka River weir began operation on May 20, on July 15 high water damaged the weir beyond repair for 2026, this was the last day of operation. The weir was not operated during coho salmon season.

Fish Creek weir operated for the full coho salmon season. The SEG of 1,200–6,000 fish was exceeded with a final count of 7,344 fish (Table 6).

The SEG for Jim Creek of 250–700 coho salmon was assessed postseason by a foot survey of McRoberts Creek, a small spawning tributary within the Jim Creek system. A survey conducted on September 28 counted 1,370 coho salmon, which exceeded the goal range (Table 6).

KING SALMON

2026 Run and Fishery Summary The 2026 UCI commercial king salmon harvest of 137 fish was 98% below the recent 20-year average of 6,840 fish (Tables 2 and 5). Fisheries across UCI were restricted or closed to reduce king salmon harvest. Using the average price of $3.77 per pound for king salmon, the estimated exvessel value of the 2026 harvest was $4,279, or >1% of the total exvessel value of all salmon in UCI (Table 3). 4

In the Central District of UCI there are five monitored king salmon stocks with escapement goals. The early and late-run Kenai River stocks are monitored with sonar, the Anchor River is monitored with a combination of sonar and weirs, and the Ninilchik River and Crooked Creek are monitored with weirs.

Total Kenai River large fish (> 75 cm mid-eye to tail fork length) early-run king salmon passage through June 30, 2026, at the river mile 14 sonar was 1,499 large king salmon. Neither the OEG of 3,900–6,600 large fish or the SEG of 2,800–5,600 large fish was achieved (Table 6). Commercial fisheries do not typically harvest this stock.

The total Kenai River large fish late-run king salmon passage through August 27, 2026, at the river mile 14 sonar was 9,803 large king salmon. ADF&G applies harvest and catch-and-release mortality estimates and spawning downstream of the sonar estimates to generate a preliminary spawning escapement estimate of 10,211 large fish. The stock of concern recovery goal of 14,250– 30,000 large fish, the OEG of 15,000–30,000 large fish, and the SEG of 13,500–27,000 large fish were not achieved in 2026 (Table 6).

The SEG (700–1,400) for natural-origin king salmon in Crooked Creek was not achieved in 2026 with a final weir count of 563 fish (Table 6). The SEG for natural-origin king salmon has not been achieved since 2020. This stock was typically only harvested by the ESSN fishery in late-June. Since the closure of the ESSN fishery, this stock is assumed to not be harvested in commercial fisheries.

Of the three southern Kenai Peninsula king salmon systems, the SEG was achieved in one system, was below in one system, and was not assessed in the third. The Anchor River achieved the SEG with a preliminary escapement estimate of 3,431 fish (SEG 3,200–6,400), and the Ninilchik River was below the natural-origin SEG with an estimate of 757 fish (SEG 900–1,600; Table 6). The Deep Creek king salmon run was not assessed due to lack of funding. These stocks are typically not harvested in commercial fisheries.

In the Northern District, there are two systems with escapement goals monitored for king salmon inseason using weirs, and multiple streams from the western side of Cook Inlet and the Susitna River Drainage are evaluated by aerial surveys.

The preliminary escapement estimate of king salmon in the Deshka River was 6,687 fish, which did not achieve the BEG of 9,000–18,000 fish. The Little Susitna River king salmon SEG of 2,100– 4,300 was not achieved in 2026, with a preliminary estimate of 691.

Aerial surveys of the indicator stocks throughout the Susitna drainage king salmon systems are pending analysis to determine whether aggregate goals have been achieved. Preliminary results indicated goals were not achieved, and the trend of low king salmon continues in these systems (Table 6).

Northern District King Salmon Fishery Northern District king salmon are primarily harvested during the directed set gillnet fishery in late May and June. Northern District commercial fisheries were restricted and closed to reduce king salmon harvest this season.

The 2026 total Northern District commercial king salmon harvest was 6 fish and 99% below the previous 20-year average harvest of 1,672 fish (Tables 4 and 5).

ESSN Fishery The 2026 preseason forecast was for a total run of 12,718 large Kenai River late-run king salmon.

5

Based on the low preseason forecast, the late-run king salmon sport fishery was closed preseason and remained closed for the 2026 season. Subsequently, the ESSN commercial fishery was closed by EO on February 11, in compliance with the Kenai River late-run king salmon stock of concern management plan (5 AAC 21.382).

PINK SALMON Pink salmon runs in UCI are even-year dominant, with odd-year average harvests typically less than even-year harvests. The 2026 commercial pink salmon harvest was 39,185 fish (Table 2), which was 91% below the average annual harvest of 428,265 fish from the most recent 20 years of even-year harvest data (Tables 4 and 5). Using an average price of $0.33 per pound, the exvessel value for the 2026 pink salmon harvest was $47,238, or 0.3% of the total exvessel value of salmon in UCI (Table 3).

CHUM SALMON

The 2026 harvest of 82,254 chum salmon was 36% below the recent 20-year average annual harvest of 127,901 fish (Table 4 and 5). Using the average price of $0.68 per pound, the exvessel value of the 2026 commercial chum salmon harvest was $423,431, or 2.6% of the total exvessel value of all salmon in UCI (Table 3). An aerial survey of Chinitna River/Clearwater Creek produced an estimate of 2,033 chum salmon within these streams, which was below the SEG range of 3,500–8,000 fish (Table 6). Commercial fishing with set and drift gillnet gear was allowed on Tuesdays and Fridays, for 12-hour periods, beginning August 28, once run timing of local chum salmon stocks have historically has been completed. This area was closed on September 30 when all of UCI closed to commercial salmon fishing for the season.
